Lewis & Clark College in Portland, Oregon, states that it aims to build a culturally, economically, socially, and geographically diverse community. To support students who might otherwise lack the resources to enroll, the college provides financial aid to international students.

Eligibility

- The college does not award athletic scholarships.
- Several named scholarships are designated exclusively for international students.

Funding Options
- Merit scholarships (automatic consideration for all applicants).
- Need‑based financial aid (details not specified in the source).

Application Process
1. Complete the International Student Application for Financial Assistance.
2. Submit official documents from employers, banks, and the tax office to support the information provided.
3. Documents can be uploaded to the L&C Portal or emailed to admissions@lclark.edu.

Deadlines
- Early Decision / Early Action: November 1
- Regular Decision: January 15

pages.title: AI Competency Framework for Students
pages.focus_keyword: AI Competency Framework for Students
pages.description: UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Students outlines 12 competencies across four dimensions—human‑centred mindset, ethics of AI, AI techniques and applications, and AI system design—structured into three progression levels (Understand, Apply, Create). The framework aims to guide educators in integrating AI learning objectives into school curricula, fostering responsible, creative, and inclusive AI literacy.
pages.content:
Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integral to everyday life, and UNESCO has released a publication to help educators embed AI learning objectives into official school curricula. The goal is to prepare students to be responsible users and co‑creators of AI, ensuring they can engage with AI safely and meaningfully.

Framework Overview

The AI Competency Framework for Students is organized around 12 competencies grouped into four dimensions:

1. Human‑Centred Mindset
2. Ethics of AI
3. AI Techniques and Applications
4. AI System Design

Each dimension is further broken down into specific learning outcomes that educators can incorporate into lesson plans and assessment strategies.

Competency Dimensions

Human‑Centred Mindset

- Encourages critical judgement of AI solutions.
- Promotes awareness of citizenship responsibilities in the AI era.

Ethics of AI

- Focuses on ethical considerations, fairness, transparency, and accountability in AI systems.

AI Techniques and Applications

- Provides foundational AI knowledge for lifelong learning.
- Covers practical applications of AI across disciplines.

AI System Design

- Emphasises inclusive, sustainable AI design principles.
- Supports students in understanding how AI systems are built and evaluated.

Progression Levels

The framework spans three progression levels:

1. Understand – Students grasp basic concepts and terminology.
2. Apply – Students use AI tools and techniques in real‑world contexts.
3. Create – Students design and develop AI solutions, demonstrating ownership and innovation.

Pedagogical Methodologies

The publication outlines domain‑specific pedagogical methodologies to support the integration of AI competencies. These include:

- Inquiry‑based learning
- Project‑based learning
- Collaborative problem‑solving
- Reflective practice

Implementation Guidance

UNESCO recommends that educators:

- Align AI competencies with existing curriculum standards.
- Provide professional development for teachers.
- Foster partnerships with industry and research institutions.
- Incorporate assessment strategies that measure understanding, application, and creation.

Conclusion

The AI Competency Framework for Students is intended to help educators prepare students as responsible, creative citizens in the era of AI. By embedding these competencies into school curricula, educators can promote critical judgement, ethical awareness, foundational knowledge, and inclusive design practices.

Known Eligibility, Funding, and Deadline

- The source text does not specify eligibility criteria, funding opportunities, or application deadlines for using the framework.

Unknowns

- It is unclear whether UNESCO offers any grants or support for curriculum implementation.
- No information is provided about the availability of teacher training programs or resource materials beyond the publication.

Source Limitations

- The information is derived solely from a single UNESCO publication dated 16 January 2026.
- No external verification or peer review is cited.
- The text may not reflect the most current updates or regional adaptations of the framework.

Read Time

Estimated reading time: 5 minutes

pages.title: The Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students: An Overview
pages.focus_keyword: The Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students: An Overview
pages.description: This article summarizes the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students, highlighting its historical context, core provisions, interpretive updates, and the associations that endorsed its footnotes. It also discusses the limitations of the available source material and identifies areas where further evidence is needed.
pages.content:
Introduction
The Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students was first adopted in 1965 by a coalition of U.S. academic associations. It has been revised in 1970, 1975, 1980, 1985, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020 to reflect changing legal and educational contexts.

Historical Context
The statement was originally endorsed by the American Association of University Professors (AAUP), the United States Student Association (USSA), and the American Association of Community Colleges (AAC). Subsequent revisions added endorsements from the American Association of University Administrators (AAUA), the American College Personnel Association (ACPA), and the Southern Association for College Student Affairs (SACSA), among others.

Core Provisions
The document outlines several key areas:

1. Freedom of Speech and Assembly on Campus
2. Non‑discrimination Policies
3. Procedural Fairness in Disciplinary Proceedings
4. Editorial Freedom of Student Publications
5. Off‑Campus Rights of Students

Interpretive Footnotes
In 2020, a set of interpretive footnotes was added to clarify the meaning of terms such as "race" and "gender". These footnotes were endorsed by a broad coalition of associations, including the American Association of University Administrators and the National Association for Women in Education.

Implementation Challenges
While the statement provides a framework, the extent to which individual institutions adopt and enforce its provisions varies. The source text does not provide data on compliance rates or enforcement mechanisms.

Source Limitations
The provided source text appears truncated and contains incomplete sentences. It also lacks citations to empirical studies or legal analyses that would support claims about the statement’s impact. Therefore, the information should be treated as preliminary and unverified.

Unknowns
- The current adoption status of the statement by individual universities.
- Empirical evidence on the statement’s effect on student outcomes.
- Any legal challenges or court rulings interpreting the statement.

Eligibility, Funding, and Deadline
The statement itself does not establish eligibility criteria, funding mechanisms, or deadlines. It is a policy document rather than a grant or program.

Conclusion
The Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students remains a foundational text for academic freedom and student conduct. However, due to incomplete source material and lack of corroborating evidence, readers should seek additional, authoritative sources before relying on the details presented here.

pages.title: Nationally Competitive Graduate Fellowships: Overview and Key Opportunities
pages.focus_keyword: Nationally Competitive Graduate Fellowships: Overview and Key Opportunities
pages.description: A concise guide to some of the most prominent national fellowships available to graduate students, highlighting eligibility, funding, and deadlines.
pages.content:
Introduction
This article summarizes a selection of nationally competitive fellowships for graduate students, drawn from a list provided by the NC State Graduate School. The information is intended to help students identify potential funding sources and understand basic eligibility and application timelines.

Key Fellowships
1. American Educational Research Association Dissertation Grants
   • Target: Advanced doctoral students in education research and related fields.
   • Funding: Supports dissertation data analysis and writing.
   • Deadline: September/October.

2. GEM Fellowship
   • Levels: MS and PhD.
   • Includes paid summer internships (some programs do not).
   • Deadline: September/October.

3. Microsoft PhD Fellowship
   • Research must align with Microsoft Research areas.
   • Requires university nomination by department chair.
   • Deadline: September/October.

4. NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP)
   • Supports outstanding graduate students in STEM disciplines.
   • Covers research‑based Master’s and doctoral degrees.
   • Deadline: September/October.

5. Woodrow Wilson Dissertation Fellowship in Women’s Studies
   • Focus: Interdisciplinary doctoral dissertations on women’s issues.
   • Deadline: September/October.

6. Fulbright U.S. Student Program (Research and English Teaching Assistantships)
   • Grants for study/research projects or English teaching abroad.
   • Deadline: October.

7. Charlotte W. Newcombe Doctoral Dissertation Fellowship
   • Final year support for PhD dissertations on ethical or religious values.
   • Deadline: November.

8. American Association of University Women (AAUW) Fellowship
   • Supports research across disciplines, emphasizing women’s advancement.
   • Deadline: November.

9. Ford Foundation Fellowships
   • Pre‑doctoral, dissertation, and postdoctoral awards.
   • Administered by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine.
   • Deadline: November.

10. Social Science Research Council International Dissertation Research Fellowships (IDRF)
    • 9–12 months of support for humanities and humanistic social science PhD students.
    • Deadline: November.

11. Critical Language Scholarship (CLS)
    • Intensive overseas language immersion for 8–10 weeks.
    • Deadline: November.

12. International Peace Scholarship
    • Scholarships for women from other countries to study in the U.S. and Canada.
    • Deadline: December.

13. National Defense Science & Engineering Graduate Fellowship (NDSEG)
    • For doctoral candidates in DoD‑interest areas.
    • Deadline: December.

14. DoD SMART Scholarship‑for‑Service Program
    • Full scholarship for STEM undergraduates and graduates.
    • Deadline: December.

15. Boren Fellowship for Study Abroad and National Security
    • Funding for U.S. graduate students to study less‑commonly taught languages.
    • Deadline: December.

16. Department of Energy Computational Science Graduate Fellowship (CSGF)
    • For U.S. citizens or permanent residents pursuing a PhD in STEM.
    • Four‑year support, renewable each summer.
    • Deadline: January.

17. Hispanic Scholarship Fund (HSF)
    • Supports students of Hispanic heritage.
    • Deadline: January.

18. National Research Council Research Associateship Programs (RAP)
    • Graduate, postdoctoral, and senior research opportunities at federal labs.
    • Deadline: February 15.

19. Smithsonian Institutional Fellowship
    • Comprehensive list of awards available on the Smithsonian website.
    • Deadline: Varies.

Eligibility, Funding, and Deadlines
• Eligibility categories are indicated as (M) for Master’s, (D) for Doctoral/PhD, and (STEM) for science, technology, engineering, and mathematics fields.
• Funding amounts and duration vary by award; specific figures are not provided in the source.
• Most fellowships require institutional nomination or assistance.
• Approximate deadlines range from September to February, with many clustered in October–December.

How to Apply
The source text notes that many fellowships require institutional nomination or assistance. Students should consult their graduate program office or the fellowship’s official website for detailed application procedures, required materials, and nomination contacts.

Limitations and Unknowns
• The list is not exhaustive; many additional national fellowships exist.
• Deadlines are listed as approximate; exact dates may change annually.
• Funding amounts, renewal policies, and specific eligibility nuances are not detailed.
• The source does not provide direct application links or contact information.
• Information is drawn from a single NC State Graduate School page and may not reflect the most current data.

Conclusion
Nationally competitive fellowships offer significant financial support and professional development for graduate students across a wide range of disciplines. Students should verify each award’s current eligibility criteria, deadlines, and application requirements through the official fellowship websites or their graduate program offices.

pages.title: Funding Resources for Graduate Geography Students at the University of Washington
pages.focus_keyword: Funding Resources for Graduate Geography Students at the University of Washington
pages.description: A concise guide to internal and external funding opportunities for graduate students in Geography at UW, summarizing eligibility, award amounts, typical deadlines, and the limits of the source information.
pages.content:
Overview
The Department of Geography at the University of Washington (UW) lists a wide range of funding sources for doctoral students, including university programs, external fellowships, travel grants, and discipline‑specific awards. The information is drawn from the department’s web page and linked resources; many entries lack specific application dates or current status.

University of Washington Internal Resources
- Howard Martin Medal: modest research support ($100‑$1,500) distributed twice yearly; eligibility limited to geography graduate students with a defined research project.
- Graduate Funding Information Service (GFIS) Blog: aggregates assistantships, scholarships, and fellowships; no specific amounts listed.
- Graduate School Fellowships, Assistantships, and Awards calendar: internal deadline not specified; includes major internal and external opportunities.
- GO‑MAP (Graduate Opportunity and Minority Achievement Program): targets under‑represented students; eligibility based on diversity contribution; amount not stated.
- UW Hires (Academic Student Employee): campus hourly positions; eligibility requires selection of “Academic Student Employee” category.
- Handshake and Office of Student Financial Aid: provide hourly campus jobs and loan information; not grant funding.
- Selected UW Fellowships & Grants:
  * Bullitt Environmental Leadership Fellowship – $50,000 per year for two years; open to graduate students interested in environmental leadership.
  * Fritz/Boeing International Research and Study Fellowships – quarter‑long grants for international research; amount not specified.
  * Graduate School Presidential Dissertation Fellowship – tuition, stipend, insurance for a quarter; nomination by department required.
  * Jacobs Research Fund (Whatcom Museum Society) – supports fieldwork on Indigenous peoples of the Americas; priority to endangered cultures; amount not listed.
  * Latino Scholars Graduate School Fellowship – $1,000 award for work benefiting Latino communities.
  * Project for Interdisciplinary Pedagogy (PIP) – cohort fellowship for doctoral teaching development; amount not disclosed.
  * UW Retirement Association Fellowship in Aging – for non‑final‑year students with interest in aging; amount not given.
  * West Coast Poverty Center Research Grants – micro‑grants up to $400 and mini‑grants $5,000‑$10,000 for community‑partner projects.

Conference Travel Support
- Graduate School Fund for Excellence and Innovation (GSFEI): travel grants of $300 for national and $500 for international conferences; application windows tied to conference dates.
- Graduate and Professional Student Senate (GPSS) Travel Grants: amounts vary; deadlines not listed.

External Fellowships and Grants (selected examples)
- AAUW American Fellowships: major fellowships for women completing dissertations; also an international fellowship for non‑U.S. citizens.
- AERA Dissertation Grants and Minority Dissertation Fellowship: small research grants; eligibility includes education policy focus.
- APS Lewis and Clark Fund: up to $5,000 for exploration/field research across disciplines.
- CAORC Multi‑Country Research Fellowship: up to $10,500 for U.S. doctoral candidates conducting regional or trans‑regional research.
- Chiang Ching‑kuo Foundation: grants and doctoral fellowships for Chinese studies; amounts not specified.
- Ford Foundation Fellowship Program: pre‑doctoral, dissertation, and post‑doctoral fellowships for teaching‑research careers.
- Fulbright‑Hays Doctoral Dissertation Fellowships: grants for dissertation research abroad in non‑Western European areas; UW internal deadline (contact gradappt@uw.edu) but external deadline not provided.
- Fulbright U.S. Student Study/Research Abroad Fellowships: ~1,800 awards annually; UW internal deadline required.
- Guggenheim Dissertation Fellowships: $20,000 for final‑year doctoral candidates; not for research expenses.
- Horowitz Foundation for Social Policy Grants: $7,500 for PhD candidates in social sciences; special awards also available.
- Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Completion Fellowships: up to $38,000 for a year for humanities or social sciences.
- NSF Geography and Spatial Sciences Doctoral Dissertation Research Improvement Awards (GSS‑DDRI): deadlines second Thursday in August and second Thursday in February; supports research on human‑environment interactions.
- SSRC Dissertation Proposal Development Fellowship (DPDF) and International Dissertation Research Fellowship (IDRF): DPDF offers early‑stage support; IDRF provides 9‑12 months (~$20,000) for non‑U.S. topics; deadlines not listed.
- Wenner‑Gren Foundation Dissertation Fieldwork Grants: up to $20,000; deadlines May 1 and November 1.
- Woodrow Wilson Foundation Newcombe Fellowship: $25,000 for 12‑month dissertation writing; tuition waiver required.
- Additional discipline‑specific awards (AAG, Antipode Foundation, American Indian Graduate Center, etc.) are listed with brief eligibility notes but without amounts or deadlines.

Eligibility and Deadlines Summary
- Most UW internal awards require departmental nomination or UW‑specific internal deadlines (often not publicly dated).
- External fellowships vary: some specify amounts and eligibility (e.g., gender, citizenship, research focus) but many omit exact deadlines.
- NSF GSS‑DDRI provides concrete deadline dates; Wenner‑Gren provides two annual deadlines; other programs require checking the original website for current cycles.

Unknowns and Source Limitations
- The source text aggregates many links but does not include current application windows, exact award amounts for many items, or confirmation that programs are still active.
- URLs are provided but not verified; some may be outdated or redirected.
- No information on the competitiveness, number of awards, or required documentation for most programs.
- The text mixes UW internal resources with national/international fellowships without clear separation of eligibility criteria specific to UW students.
- Dates for internal deadlines (e.g., GO‑MAP, Graduate School calendar) are absent, requiring prospective applicants to contact UW offices directly.

Readers should consult the original UW department pages and each fellowship’s official website for the most up‑to‑date details before applying.

pages.title: International Graduate Admissions at UC Santa Cruz: Eligibility, Funding, and Visa Requirements
pages.focus_keyword: International Graduate Admissions at UC Santa Cruz: Eligibility, Funding, and Visa Requirements
pages.description: A concise guide for prospective international graduate students at UC Santa Cruz, summarizing eligibility criteria, academic record requirements, funding options, visa procedures, and health insurance. The information is drawn from the university’s own admissions page but is presented with caution regarding source reliability.
pages.content:
Eligibility Requirements

All applicants must hold a bachelor’s degree or its equivalent from an accredited institution awarded before the quarter of admission.  A three‑year undergraduate degree is acceptable only if the applicant also possesses a postgraduate diploma, master’s degree, or higher.  Vocational, secretarial, associate, or technical degrees are not considered first degrees.  Degrees earned through extension universities are not acceptable as first degrees.  If the degree follows the Bologna Accord, the transcript must state this.

Academic Records

Applicants must submit a cumulative or overall GPA of at least 3.0 (on a 4‑point scale) from the last two years of undergraduate study, shown on official academic records.  For non‑U.S. degrees, a course‑by‑course ICAP evaluation from World Education Services (WES) is required; no exceptions are permitted.  Transcripts must be in the original language with an official, literal English translation prepared by the issuing institution or an accredited translator.  Photocopies, notarized copies, or translations lacking institutional seals are not accepted.

English Language Requirements

English proficiency requirements are listed on the university’s Test Score Requirements page.  Applicants must meet the specified scores for admission and for teaching assistant positions.

International Credential Verification

Students who studied in China or India must also submit a WES ICAP evaluation.  For Indian institutions, only the main university’s name should be entered in the application; affiliated college transcripts are not accepted.  Unofficial transcripts and translations may be uploaded to the application, but official documents must be sent to WES for final verification.

Funding Opportunities

International students may receive merit‑based financial support through departmental fellowships, teaching assistantships (TA), or research assistantships (RA).  They are not eligible for grants, loans, or work‑study awards from the UCSC Financial Aid Office.  If a department offers a TA or RA, the acceptance letter is considered sufficient proof of financial support for visa purposes.

Visa and Passport

Accepted international applicants must obtain an F‑1 student visa or a J‑1 exchange visitor visa.  After admission and submission of the Financial Certificate form, the International Student and Scholar Services (ISSS) office issues an I‑20.  Applicants must present a passport, the I‑20, proof of financial resources, and a Certificate of Eligibility (1‑20) to a U.S. Consulate.  The Department of Homeland Security’s recent policy changes affect status maintenance for F and J visa holders; applicants should review the UC Santa Cruz Global Engagement website for guidance.

Financial Support Documentation

All students must demonstrate sufficient funds for initial expenses.  International applicants must submit up‑to‑date evidence of financial support for the first academic year after formal admission.  Evidence submitted before receiving an admission letter is considered invalid.  The I‑20 Request Packet must be completed and returned to ISSS before the I‑20 is issued.

Health Insurance

International students may obtain coverage through the UC Santa Cruz Health Center.  Specific plans and enrollment procedures are available on the university’s health center website.

Unknowns and Source Limitations

• The exact application deadline for international applicants is not specified in the provided text.
• Program‑specific admission requirements (e.g., additional coursework, research experience) are not detailed.
• The text does not mention any changes to funding availability or visa regulations beyond the brief reference to the Department of Homeland Security ruling.
• The information is taken directly from a university webpage that may be updated; the date of last modification is listed as August 5, 2026, but no verification of current accuracy is provided.
• No external links or citations beyond the university’s own site are included, and the content should be cross‑checked with official admissions resources before use.

Readers are advised to consult the official UC Santa Cruz Graduate Admissions website and contact the International Student and Scholar Services office for the most current and detailed information.

pages.title: Financial Aid for International Students in the USA
pages.focus_keyword: Financial Aid for International Students in the USA
pages.description: International students in the USA face unique challenges in securing financial aid, as they are largely ineligible for federal aid. However, they can explore university aid, private scholarships, and no-cosigner loans. Understanding the differences between need-blind and need-aware admissions, as well as leveraging work opportunities, are crucial steps in funding their education.
pages.content:
### Introduction
Studying in the United States is a significant opportunity for international students, but it comes with high costs. With tuition fees at private universities reaching over $80,000 annually, international students must navigate a different financial aid landscape compared to domestic students.

### Federal Aid Limitations
International students on F-1 or J-1 visas are generally ineligible for US federal student aid, including Pell Grants and federal loans. Exceptions exist for green card holders and certain protected categories, but most international students must seek other funding sources.

### Sources of Funding
International students can access funding from personal resources, university aid, private scholarships, and loans. University aid often requires the CSS Profile instead of the FAFSA, and merit scholarships may be available based on academic performance.

### University Aid: Need-Blind vs. Need-Aware
Understanding the difference between need-blind and need-aware admissions is crucial. Need-blind schools do not consider financial need in admissions decisions, while need-aware schools do. Only a few universities, such as Harvard and MIT, offer need-blind admissions and meet full demonstrated need for international students.

### Private Scholarships and Loans
Private scholarships are available, and some lenders offer loans without a US cosigner. MPOWER Financing and Prodigy Finance provide such loans, focusing on future earning potential rather than credit history.

### Work Opportunities
International students can work on-campus and participate in programs like Curricular Practical Training (CPT) and Optional Practical Training (OPT) to earn income. However, these opportunities are limited and primarily cover living expenses.

### Government and Sponsor Scholarships
Programs like the Fulbright Foreign Student Program offer significant funding for graduate students. Students should also explore scholarships from their home countries and organizations like EducationUSA.

### Conclusion

The Developing Solutions Masters Scholarship is a flagship funding scheme launched by the University of Nottingham in 2001. It targets international students who wish to pursue a full‑time master’s (including MRes) course in September 2026 and who can propose innovative solutions that will benefit their home country.

# Eligibility
- Domiciled in Africa, India or one of the listed Commonwealth countries.
- Classified as an overseas student for fee purposes.
- Holds an offer to start a full‑time master’s (including MRes) at the University of Nottingham in September 2026.
- Must be studying in the Faculty of Engineering, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Faculty of Science or Faculty of Social Sciences.
- Not a current student or graduate of the University of Nottingham.
- Not studied and awarded a degree outside the home country.
- Not currently studying in the UK.

# Eligible Countries
Africa (all nations), Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Bangladesh, Barbados, Belize, Bermuda, British Virgin Islands, Brunei, Cayman Islands, Dominica, Falkland Islands, Fiji, Gibraltar, Grenada, Guyana, India, Jamaica, Kiribati, Malaysia, Maldives, Montserrat, Nauru, Nepal, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Pitcairn Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Sri Lanka, St Helena, St Kitts and Nevis, St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines, Tonga, Trinidad and Tobago, Tristan da Cunha, Turks and Caicos Islands, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

# Funding Details
- Scholarship covers 50% or 100% of full‑time master’s tuition fees.
- Award is for one year only; if the master’s programme is two years, the scholarship applies only to the first year.

pages.content:
## Introduction
Undergraduate international students in the United States face significant financial challenges, as most financial aid is reserved for graduate studies. According to the Institute for International Education's Open Doors 2023 report, nearly 60% of tuition payments for international students come from personal and family sources. This article examines the financial aid options available to these students, including institutional aid, scholarships, and loans.

## Eligibility
International students on nonimmigrant visas (e.g., F-1, J-1) are generally ineligible for federal financial aid, which is reserved for U.S. citizens and permanent residents. However, some private and institutional scholarships are available, often based on merit or need.

## Funding Sources
### Institutional Aid
Some universities offer financial incentives, though these are more common for graduate students. Merit-based scholarships may be available for exceptional skills or talents, but they are highly competitive.

### Scholarships and Grants
While many scholarships are limited to U.S. citizens, some databases offer opportunities for international students. It's crucial to avoid fraudulent scholarship offers and consult with university offices for verification.

### Private Loans
Private loans are rare and often require a cosigner. Interest rates and terms vary, so thorough research is essential.

### Personal Resources
Most international students rely on personal and family funding. Employment opportunities are limited by visa regulations and cannot be a primary funding source.

## Tax Considerations
Financial aid may be taxable, but exemptions exist depending on visa type and tax treaties. Consulting with a tax advisor is recommended.

## Unknowns and Limitations
The availability of financial aid varies widely between institutions, and the competitive nature of scholarships makes them uncertain. Additionally, the impact of geographic location on cost of living is a significant variable.

## Conclusion
While financial aid options for undergraduate international students are limited, understanding the available resources and planning accordingly can help mitigate costs. Students should consult with their universities and conduct thorough research to explore all potential funding avenues.

pages.content:
## Eligibility Overview
- International students on F‑1 or J‑1 visas are ineligible for federal aid (Pell Grant, subsidized loans, work‑study) because FAFSA requires U.S. citizenship or eligible non‑citizen status.
- Exceptions are narrow (refugee, asylum, certain humanitarian categories) and must be confirmed with the school’s financial‑aid office.
- DACA recipients cannot receive federal aid but may qualify for some state programs (e.g., California, Texas, New York) and many private scholarships.

## Types of Aid Available
- **Institutional merit scholarships** – offered by many universities, often automatic at admission; may require a separate application for enrolled students.
- **Institutional need‑based grants** – available at some schools; policies vary, and some institutions meet full demonstrated need for internationals.
- **State grants** – rare for F‑1 students; a few states have programs for DACA recipients.
- **Private/Foundation scholarships** – wide range, eligibility varies by country of origin, field of study, or demographic background.
- **Home‑government scholarships** – many countries fund study abroad; programs differ widely.

## Where to Start: University Programs
1. Contact the university’s international‑student office and financial‑aid office.
2. Ask:
   - Which merit scholarships are considered automatically?
   - Which scholarships require a separate application for enrolled internationals?
3. Consider negotiating aid if you have competing offers.

## External Scholarship Search Resources
- **IEFA.org** – International Education Financial Aid database, most comprehensive for internationals.
- **InternationalScholarships.com** – Organized by country of origin and field of study.
- **Scholars4Dev.com** – Focuses on students from developing countries.
- Professional and academic associations in specific fields often list scholarships.

## Major Scholarships and Typical Deadlines (2026‑2027)
- **Fulbright Foreign Student Program** – Graduate students from 160+ countries; deadline for 2027‑2028 cycle: October 6 2026 (via home‑country Fulbright Commission).
- **AAUW International Fellowships** – Women (non‑US/Canada citizens) pursuing graduate/post‑doc study; award $18,000‑$30,000; deadline: November 2026.
- **Joint Japan/World Bank Graduate Scholarship** – Students from World Bank‑member developing countries in development‑related fields; full funding; deadline varies by country.
- **Aga Khan Foundation International Scholarship** – Citizens of specific South/Central Asian and East African countries; 50% grant + 50% loan; deadline: March 2026.
- **MPOWER Women in STEM Scholarship** – International or DACA women in STEM at US/Canadian universities; $3,000 grand prize; deadline varies.
- **P.E.O. International Peace Scholarship** – Women (non‑US/Canada citizens) in graduate study; up to $12,500; deadline: December 2026.
- **DAAD Study Scholarship** – US/Canadian undergrads moving to German master’s programs; tuition + stipend; deadline: October 2026.
- **Conacyt Scholarships** – Mexican citizens for postgraduate study abroad; tuition + living costs; deadline varies.

## Application Tips
- Align essays with the scholarship’s mission, especially if it emphasizes home‑country impact.
- Apply only to programs where you meet the stated eligibility.
- Start the timeline early; many top awards require applications a year before enrollment.
- Secure recommendation letters well in advance.
- Keep a scholarship calendar and revisit opportunities each academic year.

## Unknowns and Source Limitations
- Exact award amounts for many private or foundation scholarships are not listed in the source.
- Specific eligibility criteria (e.g., GPA thresholds, citizenship restrictions) for several programs are summarized only broadly.
- Deadlines for some scholarships are noted as “varies” without precise dates, requiring verification on the sponsor’s website.
- The source text may be outdated or incomplete; it does not guarantee that listed programs are currently accepting applications.
- No direct URLs or contact information are provided; users must locate official sites independently.

## Frequently Asked Questions (selected)
- **Can I combine multiple scholarships?** Yes, many students stack institutional merit aid with private scholarships, but check each sponsor’s policy on overlapping awards.
- **What if I’m a DACA student?** Federal aid is unavailable, but some state grants and many private scholarships are open.
- **Do I need to reapply each year?** Most scholarships require annual renewal; maintain eligibility and meet reporting requirements.

- Some programs may also require a conferred post‑baccalaureate master’s or doctoral degree (excluding professional degrees) from a regionally accredited institution.
- **Returning degree‑seeking students** must apply for readmission. Requirements include:

  - New application form and $30 processing fee (waived if less than 12 months since last enrollment).
  - Official transcript of any coursework completed after the prior enrollment.
  - For students first admitted Fall 2014 or later, an acceptable standardized test score on file.
  - Good academic standing and no pending disciplinary or integrity violations.
- **Non‑degree‑seeking students** may enroll for coursework but cannot use this status as a pathway to a degree. To pursue a degree later, they must reapply as degree‑seeking.
- **Visiting students** must be actively pursuing a graduate degree at another institution and be in good standing at that home institution.
- **Senior citizens** (Arkansas residents 60 + years) may apply for graduate credit with a tuition‑waiver form; they must meet the same admission requirements as other applicants.

## Application Deadlines

pages.description: Graduate school can be expensive, but a range of funding options—assistantships, fellowships, loans, work‑study, and on‑campus jobs—can help cover tuition, fees, and living costs. pages.content:
Introduction
Graduate education involves significant financial commitments, including tuition, fees, living expenses, travel, and incidental costs. Securing funding early and understanding the various options available can ease the financial burden and allow students to focus on their studies.

Types of Funding
Assistantships
Assistantships are paid academic positions that provide tuition reimbursement in exchange for work performed for faculty, departments, or colleges. Eligibility typically requires a strong academic record and the ability to contribute to research or teaching.

Fellowships
Fellowships, also known as grants or scholarships, are competitive awards that generally do not require work in return. They are intended to fund academic study and research. Eligibility varies by program and may include academic merit, research proposals, or specific demographic criteria.

Loans
Student loans are financial obligations that must be repaid after graduation. They can be federal, state, or private and often have varying interest rates and repayment plans.

Work‑Study
The Federal/State Work‑Study program allows students to work part‑time while earning money to help pay for education. Eligibility is based on financial need and the availability of funds within the institution.

On‑Campus Jobs
Universities often list on‑campus positions on job boards such as Handshake. These roles may be related to research, teaching assistance, or administrative support.

External Jobs
Students can also seek employment outside the university through general job listings, internships, or industry positions that offer financial support.

How to Find Funding
Start Early
Funding opportunities often have deadlines that precede application periods for graduate programs. Beginning the search early—sometimes before applying to schools—can increase the likelihood of securing support.

Search University Resources
Many universities maintain internal databases or job boards where assistantships, fellowships, and on‑campus jobs are posted. Checking these resources regularly can uncover time‑sensitive opportunities.

Explore External Sources
Beyond university listings, external organizations, foundations, and government agencies offer fellowships and grants. Searching these sources can broaden the range of available funding.

Application Process
Identify Opportunities
Compile a list of potential funding sources that align with your academic goals and eligibility.

Understand Requirements
Each funding type has specific criteria, application materials, and deadlines. Carefully review these details to ensure compliance.

Submit Early
Because many deadlines are earlier than anticipated, submitting applications well in advance helps avoid last‑minute issues.

Helpful Tips
Use “Know Before You Go” Resources
Some universities provide guides that clarify financial decisions before applying to graduate programs.

Watch Funding Videos
Video tutorials can offer practical advice on navigating the funding process, including tips from students and staff.

Seek Guidance
If questions arise, contact the graduate school’s support office or use a searchable directory to find the appropriate contact person.

Conclusion
Funding graduate education requires proactive planning, thorough research, and timely application. By exploring assistantships, fellowships, loans, work‑study, on‑campus jobs, and external employment, students can create a diversified financial plan that supports their academic journey.

Known Eligibility and Funding
• Assistantships: require academic performance and work contribution.
• Fellowships: competitive, often merit‑based.
• Loans: require repayment.
• Work‑Study: based on financial need and institutional availability.
• On‑Campus Jobs: open to current students.

Deadlines
Deadlines vary by funding source and are often earlier than program application deadlines. Specific dates are not provided in the source.

Unknowns
• Exact eligibility criteria for each funding type.
• Amounts and duration of funding.
• Availability of specific assistantships or fellowships.

Source Limitations
The information is drawn from a single university webpage and has not been independently verified. No external sources were consulted, and the details may not reflect all programs, eligibility requirements, or deadlines. Readers should consult official university or funding organization websites for the most accurate and up-to-date information.

Application Process
- Most programs use the UC Graduate Admissions Application via the UC Application Portal.
- Some programs use external CAS systems (e.g., NursingCAS, OTCAS, PTCAS, ATCAS, CSDCAS, SOPHAS).

- Application fees are non‑refundable and must be paid with each submission.

Application Fees
- Domestic graduate degree programs: $65.00
- International graduate degree programs: $70.00
- Domestic graduate certificates: $20.00
- International graduate certificates: $25.00

- Automatic waivers for applicants with a bachelor’s or higher degree from listed English‑speaking countries.

- Official transcripts (or official NACES evaluations for international degrees) required after enrollment confirmation and before the start of the first term.

The timeline for applying to graduate school typically begins two years before the intended start date. During this period, applicants should research programs, prepare for standardized tests like the GRE, and gather necessary application materials.

- GRE scores
- Letters of recommendation

When selecting a graduate program, consider factors such as location, reputation, curriculum, career services, and school culture. Each of these elements can significantly impact your academic and professional experience.

### Financial Considerations
Funding graduate education can be challenging. Options include federal aid through FAFSA, merit-based scholarships, assistantships, and employer tuition reimbursement programs. It's crucial to explore all available resources to minimize financial burden.

### Interview Tips
For programs that require interviews, preparation is key. Understand your application, be ready to discuss your experiences, and ask insightful questions about the program.

### Conclusion
Applying to graduate school requires careful planning and strategic decision-making. By following a structured timeline and considering all aspects of the application process, prospective students can enhance their chances of success.

pages.description: Scholarships are a valuable resource for students seeking financial assistance for their education. This guide explores the types of scholarships available, how to find them, and the application process.
pages.content:
## Introduction
Scholarships are financial gifts that do not require repayment, making them an attractive option for students seeking to reduce the cost of their education. They are offered by a variety of sources, including schools, employers, private companies, nonprofits, and community organizations.

## Types of Scholarships
Scholarships can be categorized into several types. Merit-based scholarships are awarded based on academic achievement or a combination of academics and special talents or interests. Need-based scholarships are awarded based on financial need. Additionally, there are scholarships for specific groups, such as women, graduate students, or military families.

## Finding Scholarships
Students can find scholarships through various sources, such as the financial aid office at their school, high school counselors, libraries, and online resources. It is important to verify the legitimacy of scholarship offers and avoid scams.

## Application Process
Each scholarship has its own application requirements and deadlines. It is crucial to read the application instructions carefully, complete the application thoroughly, and submit it by the deadline.

## Scholarship Disbursement
Scholarship funds may be disbursed directly to the college to cover tuition and fees, or they may be sent directly to the student. The scholarship provider will inform the recipient of the disbursement method.

## Impact on Other Financial Aid
Receiving a scholarship may affect other financial aid, as the total aid cannot exceed the cost of attendance. Students should inform their financial aid office about any scholarships received to adjust their financial aid package accordingly.

## Conclusion
Scholarships are a valuable resource for students to help manage the cost of education. By understanding the types of scholarships available and the application process, students can increase their chances of receiving financial assistance.

## Introduction
This article synthesizes publicly available information about the graduate‑school application process. The source material is a marketing page from Sallie.com, which presents a broad overview but does not provide program‑specific data or citations. All statements are qualified accordingly.

## Typical Eligibility Requirements
- **Bachelor’s degree** from an accredited institution (often required, though some professional programs may accept equivalent experience).
- **Minimum GPA** – the source mentions a GPA requirement but does not specify a threshold; requirements vary by program.
- **Letters of recommendation** – usually 2‑3 from professors, supervisors, or professionals who can attest to academic or professional potential.
- **Personal statement / statement of purpose** – required to explain goals, motivation, and fit.
- **Resume or CV** – format depends on the program (resume for professional programs, CV for research‑oriented fields).
- **Standardized tests** – GRE, GMAT, LSAT, MCAT are common, but many programs are now test‑optional. Exact test requirements are program‑specific and not detailed in the source.
- **Prerequisite coursework or professional experience** – may be required for certain fields (e.g., engineering, health professions).

## Common Application Timeline and Deadlines
- **12‑18 months before enrollment**: Begin researching programs, building a list, and preparing for entrance exams.
- **6‑12 months before deadlines**: Register for tests, request transcripts, and ask for recommendation letters.
- **3‑6 months before deadlines**: Draft personal statements, finalize essays, and apply for scholarships.
- **Application windows**: Most graduate programs have deadlines between **November and February** for fall admission. Some use rolling admissions, extending the window.

pages.description: Graduate school can be expensive, but numerous scholarships are available to help mitigate costs. This guide explores various scholarship opportunities, eligibility criteria, and tips for maximizing financial aid.
pages.content:
## Introduction
Graduate school offers a chance to deepen your understanding of your field and can significantly enhance your career prospects. However, the cost of graduate education can be prohibitive. Scholarships provide a way to reduce financial burdens and avoid accumulating debt.

## Types of Graduate School Scholarships
Graduate school scholarships can be categorized into national, institutional, and local scholarships. National scholarships are open to most graduate students, while institutional scholarships are specific to the universities you are applying to. Local scholarships are often available through community organizations and may have less competition.

### National Scholarships
National scholarships are available to a wide range of students. Examples include the Hertz Foundation Graduate Fellowship for STEM students and the Boren Awards for those studying abroad.

### Institutional Scholarships
These scholarships are offered by the universities themselves. Contacting the financial aid office of the institution you are interested in is a good way to learn about these opportunities.

### Local Scholarships
Local organizations, such as community clubs and churches, often offer scholarships. These may have specific eligibility criteria but generally face less competition.

## Scholarships for Specific Demographics
Certain scholarships are designed for specific demographic groups, such as women and minorities.

### Scholarships for Women
- **AAUW American Fellowships**: For women pursuing doctoral degrees, with awards ranging from $8,000 to $50,000.
- **Amelia Earhart Fellowship**: For women in aerospace engineering or space sciences, offering $10,000.

### Scholarships for Minorities
- **AAA Minority Dissertation Fellowship**: For minority students completing dissertations in anthropology, offering $10,000.
- **ABA Legal Opportunity Scholarship**: For minority law students, offering $15,000.

## Tips for Finding and Applying for Scholarships
- **Research**: Use websites like Fastweb and Unigo to find scholarships.
- **Organize**: Keep track of scholarships and their deadlines.
- **Apply Broadly**: Apply to as many scholarships as you qualify for to maximize aid.

## Unknowns and Limitations
- **Eligibility Criteria**: Specific eligibility criteria for each scholarship may vary and should be verified with the scholarship provider.
- **Funding Amounts**: Award amounts can vary and may depend on financial need or other factors.
- **Deadlines**: Scholarship deadlines are not specified in the source and should be confirmed with the provider.

## Conclusion
Graduate school scholarships are a valuable resource for reducing the financial burden of advanced education. By understanding the types of scholarships available and applying strategically, students can significantly lower their educational costs.

pages.title: Finding and Applying for Scholarships
pages.focus_keyword: Finding and Applying for Scholarships
pages.description: Scholarships are financial gifts that do not require repayment. They are offered by various entities and can be merit-based or need-based. Understanding the types, application processes, and impacts on other financial aid is crucial for prospective students.
pages.content:
## Understanding Scholarships

Scholarships are financial gifts that do not require repayment. They are offered by schools, employers, individuals, private companies, nonprofits, communities, religious groups, and professional and social organizations.

### Types of Scholarships

Scholarships can be merit-based, awarded for academic achievement or special talents, or need-based, depending on financial circumstances. Some scholarships target specific groups, such as women, graduate students, or military families. The amount can vary from covering full tuition to a one-time award.

### Finding Scholarships

Scholarships can be found through various sources, including financial aid offices, high school counselors, libraries, community organizations, and employers. It is important to verify the legitimacy of scholarship offers and avoid scams.

### Application Timing

Scholarship deadlines vary, with some as early as a year before college starts. High school students should begin researching and applying during the summer between their junior and senior years.

### Application Process

Each scholarship has unique application requirements. It is essential to read the application instructions carefully, complete them fully, and adhere to deadlines.

### Scholarship Disbursement

Scholarship funds may be paid directly to the college or to the student. The scholarship provider will inform the recipient of the payment method.

### Impact on Other Financial Aid

Scholarships affect other student aid, as total aid cannot exceed the cost of attendance. Students must inform their financial aid office of any scholarships received to adjust other aid accordingly.

- **Bachelor’s degree** from a U.S. institution accredited by one of the following bodies: Higher Learning Commission (HLC), Middle States Commission on Higher Education (MSCHE), New England Commission of Higher Education (NECHE), Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities (NWCCU), Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges (SACSCOC), or WASC Senior College and University Commission (WSCUC).

## Application Process
1. Create an online application account.
2. Start a new application for each program you wish to apply to.
3. Upload required documents (transcripts, test scores, recommendation letters).
4. Pay the application fee for each program.
5. Save and submit the application.

## Deadlines
- Application deadlines differ by program.  The Graduate School encourages early submission to allow efficient processing.
- Fall‑term decisions are typically released between February and April, but exact dates vary.

- **Fellowships, grants, research assistantships, teaching assistantships, and loans** are common forms of support.
- Specific funding options and eligibility criteria are listed on each program’s page.
- The Graduate School does not provide application fee waivers; programs may offer fee waivers upon request.

- International applicants must also navigate the U.S. student visa process.
- The Graduate School evaluates credentials in‑house; external evaluations (e.g., WES) are not accepted.
- Conditional admission may be offered by some programs; contact the program for details.

pages.content:
# Harvard College Financial Aid Overview
Harvard College’s aid package is designed to cover 100 % of a student’s demonstrated financial need. The package is assembled from several sources:

- **Scholarships & Grants** – grant‑based funds that do not need to be repaid.
- **Federal and State Grants** – Pell Grants, SEOG, and Massachusetts Gilbert Grants.
- **Outside Awards** – scholarships from schools, civic groups, employers, and national programs.
- **Student Employment** – on‑campus jobs and the Federal Work‑Study Program.
- **Loans** – optional federal, Harvard‑specific, or parent loans.

## Scholarships & Grants
Harvard’s scholarships are fully grant‑based and aim to cover the remaining need after parent contribution and student employment. Sources include:
- Harvard endowment funds.
- Alumni gifts (e.g., a $150 million gift from Ken Griffin in 1989).
- General tuition revenues.
- Federal and state grants.

The aid office determines the award by first establishing the parent contribution, then factoring in student employment and any outside awards. The remaining need is covered by scholarship funds.

## Federal and State Grants
Eligible U.S. citizens or permanent residents may receive:
- **Federal Pell Grant** – eligibility determined by the FAFSA.
- **Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (SEOG)** – also based on FAFSA data.
- **Massachusetts Gilbert Grant** – for Massachusetts residents, awarded on a need basis.

Within 10 days of filing the FAFSA, students receive a Student Aid Report indicating Pell Grant eligibility.

## Outside Awards
Students can receive scholarships from:
- Secondary schools.
- Civic organizations.
- Parental employers.
- Corporations.
- National Merit Scholarship Programs.
- ROTC.

Outside awards must be reported through the Outside Awards Reporting System in the student portal. They are used to replace term‑time work expectations or, if they exceed that amount, to replace an equal amount of Harvard scholarship. They cannot replace the parent contribution.

## Student Employment
All students may work during the academic year. Typical expectations are 10–12 hours per week. Wages are paid directly to the student and can help cover personal expenses.

### Federal Work‑Study Program (FWSP)
Eligibility is indicated on the financial aid package. FWSP subsidizes wages for eligible students and is available for both term‑time and summer employment. Jobs can be found through the Student Employment Office database.

## Loans
Loans are optional and not required for the aid package. Students may choose to take out loans to cover the family contribution.

### Federal Direct Subsidized Loan
- Eligibility: U.S. citizen, permanent resident, or other eligible non‑citizen; FAFSA completed.
- Maximum amounts (full‑time): $3,500 (first year), $4,500 (sophomore), $5,500 (junior/senior).
- Interest paid by the federal government during enrollment, grace, and deferment.
- Repayment starts six months after graduation or dropping below half‑time.

### Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loan
- Same eligibility as subsidized.
- Maximum amounts (full‑time): $5,500 (first year), $6,500 (sophomore), $7,500 (junior/senior).
- Interest accrues from disbursement.

### Harvard Student Loan
- Available to all need‑based aid recipients, regardless of citizenship.
- Interest paid by Harvard during enrollment, grace, and deferment.
- Maximum $3,500 per academic year (or $1,750 per semester).
- Fixed interest rate of 4 % (5 % for loans disbursed before 07/01/2016).
- No origination or insurance fees.
- Repayment begins six months after graduation.

### Parent Loans
- No income restrictions; creditworthiness tests apply.
- Applications typically available after June 1 and should be submitted by August 1 for credit toward registration.
- Only one parent loan may be taken at a time.

## Eligibility Summary
- **Need‑based**: Demonstrated need determined by FAFSA and Harvard’s assessment.
- **Federal Grants**: U.S. citizenship or permanent residency required.
- **State Grants**: Massachusetts residency required for Gilbert Grant.
- **Loans**: Federal loans require citizenship or permanent residency; Harvard loans require need‑based aid eligibility.

## Deadlines
The source text does not provide specific application or award deadlines. Students should consult Harvard’s financial aid office or the student portal for current dates.

## Unknowns and Source Limitations
- The exact dates for FAFSA submission, grant disbursement, and loan application deadlines are not specified.
- The text does not detail the process for verifying outside awards beyond reporting them.
- No information is provided on the proportion of students receiving each type of aid or on the average award amounts.
- The source does not include links to official policy documents or up‑to‑date interest rates beyond the URLs mentioned.
- The information may be outdated; the last update noted is October 09, 2026.

## Key Takeaway
Harvard College’s aid system is structured to eliminate debt for students who qualify for need‑based aid. While scholarships and grants cover the bulk of the cost, students may supplement their aid with employment or loans. Because deadlines and some procedural details are missing, prospective students should contact the aid office for the most current guidance.

pages.content:
# International Student Financial Aid Application Forms: ISAFA and ISFCD

## Overview
International ACAC (Association for College Admission Counseling) provides two free, downloadable forms designed to standardize the financial information that international students submit to U.S. institutions:

1. **ISAFA** – International Student Application for Financial Assistance.
2. **ISFCD** – International Student Financial Certification Document.

Both forms aim to streamline the verification process required before a college can issue a Certificate of Eligibility (Form I‑20 or DS‑2019).

## Purpose of the Forms
- **ISAFA**: Allows students to present their financial standing to a college or university. The form is optional and must be accepted by the receiving institution.
- **ISFCD**: Provides a standardized method for applicants to certify available funds. Completion is required by many institutions before they can issue a Certificate of Eligibility.

## Eligibility
- Targeted at **international students** applying to **U.S. colleges and universities**.
- Applicants must be in the process of applying for institutional financial aid or a Certificate of Eligibility.
- The forms are not intended for domestic students or for institutions outside the United States.

## Funding and Support
- International ACAC does **not** provide financial assistance to students.
- The forms are offered at **no cost** to applicants.
- The primary benefit is to reduce administrative barriers and help students meet institutional financial verification requirements.

## Deadlines and Updates
- The ISAFA form was last updated by International ACAC in **August 2026**.
- The ISFCD form was also last updated in **August 2026**.
- No specific application deadlines are attached to the forms themselves; deadlines are set by individual colleges and universities.

## Known Unknowns
- **Institutional Acceptance**: It is the applicant’s responsibility to confirm whether a particular college or university will accept ISAFA or ISFCD in lieu of its own financial aid application.
- **Policy Variability**: Financial aid policies differ widely among institutions, and some may require additional documentation beyond these forms.
- **Verification Requirements**: While the ISFCD is designed to meet U.S. consular verification standards, the final decision to issue a Certificate of Eligibility rests with the individual institution.

## Source Limitations
- The information is derived from a single source (International ACAC’s website) and has not been independently verified.
- The source text does not provide direct links to the forms or detailed instructions; users should consult the official International ACAC website or contact the institution’s financial aid office for the most current forms and policies.
- No guarantees of accuracy or completeness are provided.

## Practical Tips for Applicants and Counselors
1. **Verify Acceptance**: Contact the financial aid office of each target institution to confirm whether ISAFA or ISFCD will be accepted.
2. **Complete Promptly**: Submit the forms as early as possible to allow sufficient time for institutional review and issuance of a Certificate of Eligibility.
3. **Keep Records**: Maintain copies of all submitted documentation and any correspondence with the institution.
4. **Stay Updated**: Check for any updates to the forms or institutional policies, especially if the application cycle spans multiple years.

## Conclusion
ISAFA and ISFCD are valuable tools for international students seeking to streamline the financial verification process for U.S. college admissions. While they are free and designed to reduce barriers, applicants must still navigate individual institutional requirements and confirm acceptance of these forms. Counselors should advise students to verify policies early and maintain thorough documentation throughout the application process.

pages.content:
Ph.D. in English

- Application window for fall 2027 closes on December 11 2026.
- Required materials: 
  * Statement of intent (500‑750 words) detailing professional aims and provisional field of study.
  * Three letters of recommendation, preferably from recent professors.
  * Curriculum vitae.
  * Writing sample (5 000‑7 000 words, including bibliography/works cited). A sample exceeding the limit may not be read in full; if a longer work is excerpted, a brief note explaining the context and scope is required.
- Students whose native language is not English should consult Graduate School language‑score requirements.

M.A. in English and American Literature

- Application window for fall 2027 closes on December 11 2026.
- Application requirements are identical to the Ph.D. program.
- The M.A. program is open only to Notre Dame and St. Mary’s College graduates and to students from other institutions with portable funding (e.g., international students with government funding or service members with tuition scholarships).
- Students who do not meet those criteria but wish to pursue graduate studies in English at Notre Dame should apply directly to the Ph.D. program.

MFA in Creative Writing

- Application window for fall 2027 closes on December 11 2026.
- Required materials: 
  * Writing sample: 25‑30 pages of prose (short fiction, nonfiction, novel excerpt) or 20 pages of poetry (20 short poems or several longer poems up to the page limit). The same sample may be used for both prose and poetry applications if it falls between genres.
  * Statement of intent (≤ 1 000 words) discussing approach to writing, inspirations, purpose, goals during and after the MFA, and the thesis project.
  * Three letters of recommendation from former undergraduate or graduate teachers or other writing professionals.
  * Transcripts from all postsecondary institutions attended (unofficial transcripts acceptable for evaluation; official transcripts required upon acceptance).
- Students whose native language is not English should consult Graduate School language‑score requirements.

Funding for Ph.D.

- Five‑year funding package: full tuition scholarship, competitive stipend, health benefits, and generous funding for research and conference travel.
- Additional support: automatic consideration for premium fellowships (Notebaert, Presidential, Deans’ for underrepresented groups, Gaia for Latino studies). Students may also apply for dissertation fellowships from the university and external organizations.
- Research and travel grants: $2 000 from the department toward research and conference travel for all entering students; $350 per year for years 1‑3; $700 per year for years 4‑5.
- Sixth‑year postdoctoral fellowship (5 + 1) available after completing the Ph.D., offering a salary, professional‑development funds, and health benefits.

Funding for MFA

- Full tuition waiver.
- Fellowship providing a full stipend.
- Health‑insurance subsidy.
- Teaching, editorial, and publication experience.
- Graduating MFAs may apply for the Sparks Prize, which awards one student $37 000 to live and write for a third year; requirements are residency in South Bend and one public reading.

Funding for M.A.

- Full tuition scholarship for the two‑year program.
- Students benefit from the low cost of living in South Bend.

Eligibility and Application Deadline

- All programs share the same application deadline: December 11 2026 for fall 2027 admission.
- Ph.D. and MFA applicants must meet general Graduate School requirements.
- M.A. applicants must be Notre Dame or St. Mary’s College graduates or have portable funding.

- Eligibility: Academic performance, financial need, extracurriculars, nationality, and field of study are repeatedly cited.

pages.description: Scholarships are financial gifts that do not require repayment, offered by various organizations. This guide explores types of scholarships, how to find and apply for them, and their impact on other financial aid.
pages.content:
## Introduction
Scholarships are financial gifts that do not require repayment. They are offered by schools, employers, individuals, private companies, nonprofits, communities, religious groups, and professional and social organizations.

## Types of Scholarships
Scholarships can be merit-based, awarded for academic achievement or special talents, or need-based, depending on financial circumstances. Some scholarships target specific groups, such as women, graduate students, or military families. Scholarships vary in amount, from covering full tuition to providing a one-time award.

## How to Find Scholarships
Scholarships can be found through various sources, including financial aid offices, libraries, and online resources. It's important to verify the legitimacy of scholarship offers and avoid scams. Free sources of scholarship information include:
- College financial aid offices
- High school or TRIO counselors
- Libraries
- Foundations and community organizations
- Professional associations
- Ethnicity-based organizations
- Employers

## When to Apply
Scholarship deadlines vary, with some as early as a year before college starts. High school students should begin researching and applying for scholarships during the summer between their junior and senior years. If deadlines are missed, it's still possible to find scholarships with later deadlines.

## How to Apply
Each scholarship has specific application requirements. It's crucial to read the application instructions carefully, complete the application fully, and meet the deadline.

## How Scholarships Are Paid
Scholarship funds may be disbursed directly to the college or to the student. The scholarship provider should inform the recipient of the payment method.

## How Scholarships Affect Other Aid
Scholarships impact other student aid, as total aid cannot exceed the cost of attendance. Recipients must inform their school of any scholarships received to adjust their financial aid package accordingly.

Why Scholarships Matter for Graduate School

Graduate programs can be expensive, with tuition, books, and living expenses adding up quickly. Scholarships provide a way to reduce debt, allowing students to focus on their studies and future careers.

Types of Scholarships for Graduate Students

Merit‑Based Scholarships
  • Awarded for academic achievement, leadership, or special talents.
  • Often require a strong GPA or portfolio.

Need‑Based Scholarships
  • Designed for students with financial need.
  • Usually require financial documentation or FAFSA® information.

Program‑Specific Scholarships
  • Offered by universities or departments for particular fields (e.g., STEM, education, public health).

No‑Essay Scholarships
  • Quick application process.
  • Examples from the source: $5,000 Grad School No Essay Scholarship, $2,000 No Essay Scholarship (due 10/31/26), "Be Bold" No Essay Scholarship $25,000 (due 10/31/26), ScholarshipOwl No Essay Scholarship $50,000 (due 10/31/26), The Scholarships360 $10,000 No Essay Scholarship (due 10/31/26), Featured Niche $50,000 No Essay Scholarship (due 12/31/26).

How to Find and Apply for Scholarships

1. Start with trusted tools such as Scholly Scholarships and Scout College Search.
2. Use filters to narrow by degree type, major, and eligibility.
3. Keep a spreadsheet of deadlines and requirements.
4. Apply early; many awards are first‑come, first‑served.

Eligibility Requirements (general)

• Proof of enrollment or acceptance to a graduate program.
• Academic transcripts or GPA.
• Personal statement or essay (unless the award is no‑essay).
• Letters of recommendation.
• Financial documents for need‑based awards.

Deadlines and Application Timelines

• Most scholarships have deadlines between January and May.
• Some awards are open year‑round (e.g., the $5,000 Grad School No Essay Scholarship).
• Specific deadlines from the source include 10/31/26 for several no‑essay awards and 10/26/26 for several hospitality‑related endowed scholarships.

Tips for Winning Graduate School Scholarships

• Tailor each application to the specific award.
• Highlight your unique story, goals, and challenges.
• Proofread all materials; typos can hurt.
• Seek feedback from mentors or peers.

Additional Resources for Graduate Students

• Scout College Search for program matching.
• Scholarships by Major for field‑specific awards.
• Scholarships for Adults and Women for targeted support.
• LGBTQ Scholarships for inclusive funding.
• Scholarships by State for location‑based opportunities.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: When are scholarship application deadlines?
A: Each scholarship has its own deadline; keep track of dates to avoid missing opportunities.

Q: Do I need to know which college I’ll attend before applying?
A: Not necessarily, but some awards may require proof of enrollment after acceptance.

Q: Is there a limit on how many scholarships I can apply for?
A: No; applying to multiple increases your chances.

Q: Do all scholarship applications require an essay?
A: No; many no‑essay awards exist.

• Specific eligibility criteria for each listed scholarship are not fully detailed.
• Deadlines and award amounts could change; verify with the issuing organization.
• No independent verification of the accuracy of the listed data.

Conclusion

Graduate scholarships are a valuable resource for reducing the financial burden of advanced study. By using reputable search tools, staying organized, and applying early, students can increase their chances of securing funding. Always verify details directly with the scholarship provider before submitting an application.
